new_statements.rule_in_words: Sandawe is described purely as a lexical tone language (underlying H vs L on morae/syllables, with downstep, tone spread and largely predictable tone melodies); none of the five accessible primary descriptions posits word stress or an accent position. The only stress remark is that Swahili penultimate stress is borrowed as a Sandawe high tone.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. Kagaya 1993 (intro) notes the vowel of a word-initial syllable tends to be lengthened in isolation forms; Elderkin 1989 and Steeman 2012 describe word-level pitch registers ('word levels') assigned by syntax/information structure, not stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Tone statements concern the phonological word (root/stem plus suffixes and clitics); downdrift applies within the phonological word (Steeman 2012 p. 48). No citation-form stress domain is defined because no stress is described.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe Sandawe (sand1273, ISO sad). Hunziker, Hunziker & Eaton 2008 is based mainly on one speaker from Magambua (western dialect); Eaton 2010 and Steeman 2012 draw on both western and eastern dialect speakers. No separate dialect glottocodes involved.

new_statements.quote: [sec. 1.2, PDF p. 4] The following tone markings are used: [a-acute] high, [a-grave] low, [a-hacek] rising, [a-circumflex] falling, [grave] floating low tone. [...] [fn. 11, PDF p. 5] Except under certain conditions, the tone pattern of an uninflected verb in the realis is neutralised in that it becomes an all low-toned pattern (c.f. the tonal system for Sandawe described in Elderkin, 1989). [...] [sec. 4.2, PDF p. 14] That is, the verb occurs with a low tone pattern and contrasts with the high tone pattern of the immediately preceding focused constituent. [...] Thus the subject is given prominence in the utterance as it alone has the highest pitch.

new_statements.relation_note: Consistent with the existing statement from Hunziker, Hunziker & Eaton 2008 / Eaton 2010 (two underlying tone levels H and L with downstep; tone language, no stress statement). Eaton 2005 uses the same SIL (Hunziker & Hunziker) analysis, marks H/L plus rising/falling contours and a floating L, and likewise says nothing about stress. The catalog record itself has an empty rule (world-2026-09-17), so nothing is contradicted; this work adds no stress placement.
new_statements.rule_in_words: The paper is a syntax/information-structure study (focus marking by inflection, constituent order and tone). Its phonological preliminaries give consonant and vowel charts and a tone transcription with high, low, rising, falling and floating low tones; lexical stems and affixes carry 'basic tone patterns', verb tone patterns can be neutralised to all-low, and focus is signalled partly by tone/pitch ('prominence' is used only in the information-structure sense, realised as the focused constituent having the highest pitch). The words 'stress' and 'accent' do not occur anywhere in the 27 pages; nothing is said about word stress.
new_statements.exceptions: none (no stress statement); tonal detail only: nasal vowels phonologically long; realis uninflected verbs neutralise to all-low tone except under certain conditions; sentence-initial irrealis verb must keep its underlying tone pattern.
new_statements.identity_note: Data from a single main consultant, Nestori Michaeli of Magambua, Usandawe (Kondoa district), collected June-September 2000; no dialect distinction is drawn. The PDF read is the author's preprint of the OPiL 1 paper (a selection from her 2002 Reading PhD thesis 'A grammar of focus in Sandawe'), unpaginated.
